title: JVM Architecture and Memory
description: The JVM's stack and heap, object references, garbage collection, and a conceptual look at class loading.
objectives: Understand the stack/heap split and what lives where
Understand how garbage collection reclaims memory
Understand memory leaks conceptually, even with garbage collection
Understand class loading at a conceptual level

content.heading: Stack, Heap, and References
content.body:
Each thread has its own call stack, holding a stack frame per active method call — local variables (including primitives, stored directly) and the reference values pointing to objects, plus bookkeeping about where to resume execution once the call returns. Frames are pushed on call and popped on return, giving stack memory very fast, predictable allocation/deallocation.

The heap is a single, shared memory region (across all threads) where every object (everything created with new) actually lives — its fields, whatever their types. A reference variable, whether it's a local variable on the stack or a field inside another object on the heap, just holds the address of an object on the heap; multiple references can point to the same heap object, exactly as covered in earlier OOP lessons.

content.heading: Garbage Collection and Class Loading
content.body:
Java's garbage collector automatically reclaims heap memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable from any live reference (traced from a set of 'roots': local variables on active stacks, static fields, etc.) — the programmer never explicitly frees memory, unlike C. This eliminates whole categories of bugs (double free, use-after-free) but doesn't eliminate memory problems entirely: a 'memory leak' in Java means objects that are technically still reachable (e.g., through a growing static collection that's never cleared) but functionally unused, so the garbage collector correctly leaves them alone, and memory usage grows unboundedly anyway.

Class loading is the process by which the JVM finds a compiled .class file's bytecode, verifies it, and prepares it for execution the first time that class is actually needed at runtime (not necessarily when the program starts) — the class loader subsystem, along with the method area/metaspace (where class-level data like static fields and method bytecode itself is stored, distinct from both the stack and the per-object heap), rounds out the JVM's core memory architecture.

content.explanation: Every Object added to the static cache list remains reachable (via cache) for as long as the program runs, so the garbage collector can never reclaim it — a textbook example of a Java memory leak despite automatic garbage collection.

keyPoints: Each thread has its own stack (frames, locals, references); the heap holds all objects, shared across threads
Garbage collection reclaims heap memory for objects no longer reachable from any live reference
A Java 'memory leak' means objects stay reachable (e.g., via a growing static collection) but are functionally unused
Class loading happens on first use, not necessarily at program startup, and loads bytecode from .class files
commonMistakes: Assuming garbage collection makes memory leaks impossible in Java
Accumulating objects in a long-lived static collection (like a cache) without ever removing entries
Confusing stack memory (fast, per-thread, per-call) with heap memory (shared, holds all objects)
